Running every question against every chunk multiplies cost and latency for each resident question, which suits a one-off analysis rather than an interactive service (C). Dropping chapters leaves questions about the missing sections unanswerable, and caching does not change that (D).

question: A construction firm's site engineers use Claude Code, and each week they repeat a nine-step safety-incident write-up: pull together what was discussed in the session about the incident, fill the firm's template, and run a short check script. The firm wants it consistent, started with one short command, and shared without anyone copying files around. The procedure depends on what the engineer and Claude already established earlier in the same session. What should the firm set up?

options.A: A project skill in the repository's skills folder, holding the template and check script, committed so the team gets it.
options.B: A project subagent definition that carries the template and the steps, which engineers start whenever an incident needs a write-up.
options.C: A personal slash command file kept in each engineer's home directory, copied from a shared drive together with the template.
options.D: A new section in the project's CLAUDE.md that lists the nine steps and the template, read by Claude when each session starts.

rationale: (A) satisfies the deciding detail: a skill runs in the current conversation, so it can use what was established earlier, it is invoked with a short name, and committing it under the project's skills folder shares it with the team. (B) runs in a fresh, isolated context that does not see the session history, which suits verbose side tasks but not this procedure. (C) is personal in scope and needs manual copying, which the firm wants to avoid. (D) loads the full procedure into every session although it is used only for incidents, and it gives no single command to start it.

question: A packaging manufacturer's quality team uses Claude to sort supplier defect reports into 30 defect codes, and the model version in production has been deprecated, with retirement nine weeks away. The team holds 3,000 past reports whose correct codes inspectors confirmed, and a wrong code sends a shipment to the wrong inspection line. How should they plan the move to the recommended replacement?

options.A: Change the model name to the recommended replacement in production and staging today, and correct codes that inspectors later flag.
options.B: Score the replacement on the 3,000 confirmed reports now, fix regressions in the prompt, then move traffic in stages before retirement.
options.C: Stay on the current version until the last week before retirement, then switch in one release once the replacement looks stable.
options.D: Keep calling the retiring version and add an automatic fallback that resends failed requests to the replacement after retirement.

rationale: A deprecated model keeps working until its retirement date, after which requests fail, so the team has nine weeks to gather evidence. Running the replacement on the confirmed reports shows which codes regress, the prompt can be fixed before customers are affected, and a staged shift limits exposure ((B)). Switching everywhere today ((A)) treats the vendor's recommendation as proof and lets inspectors find the regressions. Waiting until the last week ((C)) leaves no time to fix what the comparison reveals. A fallback after retirement ((D)) sends the first replacement traffic through an unmeasured path, at the moment the old model stops answering.

question: An HR team is building an MCP server so a Claude assistant can answer employees' questions about their own pay slips and leave balance. The payroll database also holds colleagues' salaries and write tables for bank details. The prototype connects with the database administrator account because that was quickest. Before the pilot, the security lead wants the server's data access limited to what the feature needs. What should the team do?

options.A: Keep the administrator account and add a system prompt rule limiting the assistant to the signed-in employee's records.
options.B: Give the server its own database role with read access to the pay slip and leave views only, scoped to the signed-in employee.
options.C: Expose one run-query tool and have the security team review the generated SQL in the logs on a weekly basis.
options.D: Put the server on a private network segment and keep the administrator account, so outsiders cannot reach it.

rationale: (B) applies least privilege where it is enforced: a stolen or misused credential can read only the views the feature needs, which is the scope-minimisation guidance in the MCP security best practices. (A) relies on the model to restrain itself while the credential can still read and write everything. (C) adds after-the-fact auditing around an over-broad tool, so damage happens before anyone looks. (D) limits who can reach the server, not what a call through it can do, so any bug or injected instruction still runs with administrator rights.

question: A commercial insurer extracts policy details from scanned renewal letters using Claude and a JSON schema in which the renewal date is a required date field. Some letters never state a renewal date, and the model fills the field with plausible invented dates that reach the underwriting system, whose loader rejects records with a missing key. The team wants the invented dates gone without breaking the loader. What should they change?

options.A: Remove the renewal date from the list of required fields so the model can leave it out when a letter is silent about it.
options.B: Keep the field required but let its type accept null, and describe null as the value for a letter with no date.
options.C: Keep the schema and add a date format constraint to the field so that the model returns dates in a valid layout.
options.D: Keep the schema and check each returned date against the letter text, discarding records whose date cannot be found there.

rationale: A required field with a plain date type forces the model to emit some date even when the letter has none, so the schema must give it a legitimate way to say nothing was stated; a null that stays inside a required field also keeps the key present for the loader ((B)). Making the field optional ((A)) removes the invented dates but produces records with a missing key, which this loader rejects. A format constraint ((C)) guarantees well-formed dates, not truthful ones. Checking against the letter ((D)) catches some inventions after the fact, but discards records instead of reporting an absent date.

question: A customs broker uses Claude to suggest tariff codes for about 9,000 shipment documents a day. Roughly 300 of them are flagged as perishable cargo and need a suggestion within ten minutes, while the rest only have to be finished before a filing cut-off thirty hours later. The team wants to pay as little as the deadlines allow. How should it route the work?

options.A: Put the whole day's documents into one Message Batch, and poll it often to pick up the perishable ones early.
options.B: Send the whole day's documents through the standard Messages API and pace the calls to stay under the account's rate limits and quotas.
options.C: Submit two Message Batches, a small one for the perishable documents and a large one for the rest, and poll the small one each minute.
options.D: Send the perishable documents through the standard Messages API and submit the remaining ones as a Message Batch right away.

rationale: Batches are cheaper but come with no latency guarantee: they usually finish within an hour and expire after 24 hours, which fits the thirty-hour cut-off for the bulk of the work but not a ten-minute need. Real-time calls for the 300 urgent documents and a batch for the rest match each deadline at the lowest cost ((D)). One batch for everything ((A)) puts the perishable documents on a path that can take hours. Real-time calls for everything ((B)) meet every deadline but pay full price for documents that can wait. A small separate batch ((C)) is still a batch, so frequent polling does not make it finish sooner.

question: A hotel group's concierge assistant has two tools: one returns a guest's loyalty profile and preferences, the other returns their stays and room bookings. When guests ask what day they check out, the assistant often calls the profile tool and then says it cannot find the date. Both descriptions currently read 'Looks up a guest'. The team can edit only the tool definitions this sprint, not the backend or the prompt. What change fixes the confusion?

options.A: Rewrite each description to say what it returns, when to use it and when to use the other tool, naming stay dates.
options.B: Merge the two tools into one lookup tool with a mode parameter, and let the assistant choose the mode from the question.
options.C: Force the booking tool on each turn with the tool choice setting, so profile calls can no longer be picked for date questions.
options.D: Shorten both descriptions to a single clear verb phrase, so the assistant has less text to misread when it picks a tool.

rationale: (A) works within the constraint and targets the cause: the docs call detailed descriptions the most important factor, covering what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, and what it returns. (B) is a recognised consolidation practice, but it needs backend changes the team cannot make this sprint. (C) would block legitimate profile questions, since forcing a tool applies to the whole request. (D) makes the ambiguity worse, because the problem is too little information in the descriptions, not too much.

question: A property-management platform lets landlords chat with a Claude assistant about their leases. The assistant calls a lookup tool that takes a landlord ID and a unit number, both filled in by the model from the conversation. During testing, one landlord typed another landlord's ID and received that person's lease terms. The team must keep each customer's data inside that customer's own calls. What should they do?

options.A: Add a line to the system prompt telling the assistant to look up records for the signed-in landlord's ID and to refuse other IDs.
options.B: Send each answer through a second Claude call that checks whether it names a landlord other than the signed-in user.
options.C: Have the server take the landlord ID from the authenticated session and apply it to each query, outside the tool's inputs.
options.D: Create a separate workspace and API key for each landlord so that their usage and prompt caches are kept apart.

rationale: The tool's inputs are written by the model, which user text can steer, so the tenant must come from something the user cannot influence: the authenticated session, applied by the server ((C)). A prompt rule ((A)) asks the model to behave but enforces nothing when it is persuaded otherwise. A second check ((B)) runs after the other landlord's data has already been fetched and can miss it. Separate workspaces and keys ((D)) isolate usage and caches at the API, but the lookup tool still reads the platform's own database with whatever ID it is given.

question: A manufacturer's accounts-payable team extracts line items and totals from about 40,000 supplier invoices a month. Most invoices are clean, but a few formats are messy and nobody can predict which in advance. Every extraction can be checked mechanically, because the line items must add up to the stated total. Costs keep climbing on the largest model. How should the team structure the pipeline?

options.A: Send invoices with many pages or unusual file types to the larger model and keep the remaining invoices on the small one.
options.B: Ask the small model to report a confidence score with each extraction and escalate those below a threshold.
options.C: Run a small model first, check each result against the stated totals and re-run failures on a larger model.
options.D: Keep the whole volume on the larger model at a low effort setting and spot-check a weekly sample of results.

rationale: A mechanical check gives a reliable failure signal, so the cheap model handles the clean majority and only the extractions that fail the arithmetic pay for the larger model (C). Page count and file type are weak stand-ins for messiness, so hard invoices slip through on the small model while clean ones are escalated (A). Self-reported confidence is the fallback when no objective check exists, but here the totals check is stronger (B). Keeping every invoice on the larger model at low effort still bills the full volume at the larger tier, and with no mechanical check or re-run the hard invoices are only spot-checked (D).

question: A property-management SaaS runs the Claude Agent SDK in a few shared containers that serve many landlords. Each session reads and writes the container's default memory and settings locations, and last week an agent working for one landlord quoted a dispute that belonged to another landlord's tenants. The team wants a fix that still holds if a prompt instruction is ignored. What should it change?

options.A: Add a rule to the system prompt telling the agent to use the notes of the landlord it is currently serving and to ignore the rest.
options.B: Encrypt the shared notes directory at rest with a key held by the platform team, so that outside readers cannot open the files.
options.C: Run a second Claude call on each reply to detect names or addresses from a different landlord and block the replies that contain them.
options.D: Give each landlord a separate configuration directory and working directory so that no notes or settings are shared.

rationale: The leak comes from files that all sessions in a container read by default, so separate configuration and working directories per tenant remove the shared state itself, whatever the model does ((D)). A prompt rule ((A)) depends on the model obeying it. Encryption at rest ((B)) protects against outside readers, but the agent process inside the container can still open the files. A second model screening replies ((C)) is a probabilistic check after the context is already mixed.

question: A property-management company has Claude route tenant requests into five categories: plumbing, electrical, heating, pests and lease questions. Its prompt contains eight examples, all of them dripping taps and blocked drains. In testing, requests about mice and about lease renewals are often labelled plumbing, although the category definitions are clear. The team wants better routing without changing the model. What should it change?

options.A: Keep the eight examples and extend them to about forty by adding more tenant requests about leaks, drains and taps.
options.B: Drop the examples and rewrite the category definitions as long paragraphs that describe typical requests for each category.
options.C: Add a keyword filter after the model that rewrites the label when a request contains words such as mouse, ants, rats or lease.
options.D: Replace the examples with a short, varied set that covers each category, including borderline requests, in one format.

rationale: (D) addresses the cause: the docs say examples should be relevant and diverse enough that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns, and eight plumbing-only examples teach that every request is plumbing. (A) adds volume but keeps the same narrow pattern. (B) is reasonable when no examples exist, yet it discards the strongest steering tool for format and boundaries, and the stem says the definitions already read clearly. (C) patches symptoms with brittle rules and misses requests phrased without those words.

question: A hospital network wants a Claude assistant to answer clinicians' questions using its staff-scheduling system, which is reachable only from inside the hospital's private network and needs the staff member's single sign-on identity. The assistant's backend is a service the hospital hosts itself. An engineer proposes enabling Anthropic's web fetch tool and pointing it at the scheduling system's internal URLs. Which approach should the team take?

options.A: Enable web fetch and add the scheduling domain to its allowed domains, so Anthropic's servers retrieve the pages for Claude.
options.B: Define a client tool whose handler runs inside the network, calls the scheduling API as the user, and returns the result.
options.C: Use the code execution tool and let Claude write a script that calls the scheduling API from inside its sandbox.
options.D: Register the scheduling system with the MCP connector in the Messages API, so Anthropic's API connects to it directly.

rationale: (B) fits because client tools run in the application the hospital controls, so the call can reach the internal API with the user's identity and Claude only sees the returned result. (A) fails because web fetch is a server tool that runs on Anthropic's infrastructure, which cannot reach private addresses. (C) fails because the code execution sandbox has no network access and is not on the hospital's network. (D) fails because the connector requires a server that is publicly exposed over HTTP, which an internal-only system is not.

question: A city government's IT department deploys managed settings for Claude Code that deny the curl command on its workstations. A data analyst in the transport office needs curl to fetch open-data files and has added an allow rule for it to the committed project settings, but Claude Code still refuses. She is weighing other places to put the rule. Which action will actually resolve the problem?

options.A: Move the allow rule into her local project settings file, which ranks above the committed project file.
options.B: Ask the administrators to change the managed policy, which sits above the other settings locations.
options.C: Pass the allow rule through the command-line settings option, which takes precedence over the project and user files.
options.D: Copy the allow rule into her user settings file, which applies across the projects on her own workstation.

rationale: Managed settings are the top level of the precedence stack, and a deny cannot be lifted by an allow rule at a lower level, so only a change to the managed policy itself helps ((B)). The local project file ((A)) outranks the committed file but is still below managed settings. The command-line settings option ((C)) overrides the project and user files and still sits below managed settings. A user settings file ((D)) is the lowest of the personal locations and widens the rule to every project without lifting the deny.

question: An education-technology company has Claude write feedback comments on student essays. Teachers like a particular house voice (warm, specific, one next step) but struggle to put it into words, and the current prompt with eight written style rules still produces generic comments. Essays and their problems vary widely. The team wants the house voice without changing the model. What should they add?

options.A: Add three to five real teacher comments that cover different essay problems, wrapped in example tags.
options.B: Expand the written rules to forty detailed points, each describing one trait of the house voice.
options.C: Add one long teacher comment for a single strong essay, and ask Claude to match its structure and phrasing closely.
options.D: Have Claude draft each comment, critique it against the eight rules and rewrite it in a second pass.

rationale: A voice that resists description is best shown: a few relevant, diverse examples in example tags let Claude infer the tone and structure, while the variety keeps it from copying one pattern (A). More rules help only when the voice can be described, and the teachers say it cannot (B). A single long example anchors every comment to one essay type and invites near-copies (C). Self-critique against the same rules cannot add the quality the rules fail to capture (D).

question: A medical-device maker lets developers use Claude Code on firmware that is under regulatory audit. Auditors require a timestamped record of each file Claude edits with no gaps, and the current CLAUDE.md instruction to log each edit is skipped when sessions get long. The team wants a complete record that does not depend on the model remembering to write it. What should they add?

options.A: A PostToolUse hook matched to the file edit and write tools that appends the file path and a timestamp to the audit log.
options.B: A longer CLAUDE.md section with the log format and a reminder to record each edit, placed at the top of the file.
options.C: A custom slash command that developers run at the end of a session to scan git status and write the audit log.
options.D: A dedicated logging subagent that Claude is told to call after it finishes each group of edits in a session.

rationale: A hook runs as code at a fixed point in the tool lifecycle, so the entry is written after every matching edit whether or not the model remembers ((A)). A longer CLAUDE.md ((B)) is still an instruction the model can skip. A slash command run at the end ((C)) relies on a developer remembering it and sees only the final state, so intermediate or reverted edits leave gaps. A logging subagent ((D)) is called only when the model decides to call it.

question: A news publisher's fact-check assistant builds each request in this order: the current time to the second and the editor's name, then a 9,000-token style and sourcing handbook, then the article under review, then the editor's question. The handbook never changes. The team marked the article block for caching, yet usage shows cache writes and no reads. What should they change so the handbook is served from the cache?

options.A: Put the cache marker on the editor's question so the whole request is stored and can be reused later.
options.B: Keep the order, mark the time and name line for caching and request the one-hour lifetime to keep it longer.
options.C: Move the time and editor name after the handbook and mark the last block of the handbook for caching.
options.D: Keep the order and move the cache marker onto the handbook block so the handbook alone is stored.

rationale: The cached prefix has to be identical up to the marked block, so the changing time and name must come after the handbook and the marker belongs on the handbook's last block (C). A marker on the question writes a new entry on every request that no later request can match (A). Marking the line with the time and name caches content that differs each time, and a longer lifetime cannot make it match (B). Marking only the handbook does not help while the changing line sits in front of it, because the prefix before the marker still differs on every request (D).

question: A telecom's support assistant puts each customer email between XML-style tags in the prompt and asks Claude to summarise whatever sits inside them. Customers often paste router configuration snippets, and some pastes contain the literal closing tag of the wrapper followed by text that reads like an instruction, which Claude then sometimes follows. The team wants to remove this break-out risk at its source. What should it change?

options.A: Add a sentence to the system prompt telling Claude to treat the tagged text as data and to ignore instructions found inside it.
options.B: Encode the email as a JSON string, or escape its angle brackets, so that a pasted tag cannot end the data section.
options.C: Scan incoming emails for phrases such as ignore previous instructions, and reject the messages that contain one of them.
options.D: Rename the wrapper to a longer, unusual tag name, so customers are unlikely to paste the matching closing tag.

rationale: (B) removes the cause: the docs recommend JSON-encoding untrusted content so that an attacker cannot close a quote or tag to break out into an instruction context. (A) is a useful extra layer, but once a pasted closing tag ends the data section, the text that follows sits outside the area the sentence refers to. (C) matches known phrases only and does nothing about the delimiter itself, so a reworded instruction still gets through. (D) relies on obscurity; the tag name can leak, and pasted markup could still contain it.

question: An airline's operations-control tool generates a 500-word irregular-operations brief that the duty manager watches appear and cannot act on until it is complete. It takes about 25 seconds on the company's top-tier model, which offers fast mode, and tests show quality dipping on smaller models for these briefs. Extra spend is approved. How can the team shorten the wait without changing the output quality?

options.A: Move the briefs to the Message Batches API, which lowers the cost per brief and handles heavy volume.
options.B: Step down to the next smaller model tier with the same prompt and accept a small change in brief quality.
options.C: Lower the effort setting to low on the same model so it spends fewer tokens on reasoning for each brief.
options.D: Enable fast mode on the same model, which speeds up output generation at a premium price.

rationale: Fast mode runs the same model with a faster inference configuration, raising output tokens per second at premium pricing, and the stem allows the extra spend while ruling out a quality change (D). The Batches API trades speed for a discount and is meant for work nobody is waiting on, which is not this case (A). A smaller tier changes quality, which the tests rule out (B). A lower effort setting trades some capability for speed and cost, so it also changes what the briefs contain (C).

question: A restaurant group's procurement assistant helps managers reorder supplies in sessions that are weeks apart. Managers keep re-explaining their approved suppliers and preferred delivery days, but the supplier price quotes the assistant fetches go out of date within a few days. The team is adding the memory tool and must decide what the assistant writes to it. Which choice is best?

options.A: Save the complete tool results from each session, quotes included, so that later sessions can read the same information again.
options.B: Skip memory and load the managers' complete order history into the context at the start of each session instead.
options.C: Save a summary of each session, quotes included, and load the three most recent summaries when the next session starts.
options.D: Save the confirmed supplier choices and delivery-day preferences, and fetch fresh price quotes again in each session.

rationale: Standing preferences and confirmed decisions stay valid for weeks, so they are worth carrying across sessions, while quotes expire in days and are better fetched live each time ((D)). Saving full tool results ((A)) fills memory with stale prices that the assistant may trust. Loading the order history ((B)) puts a large record in every context and still does not hold what managers say about preferences. Session summaries with quotes ((C)) carry out-of-date prices forward and bury the lasting facts.

question: A market-research firm's Claude agent reads competitors' public web pages and PDFs. It also holds a tool that reads a client's confidential pricing sheet and a tool that posts to a shared channel. The team accepts that a hostile page may eventually slip an instruction past the model, and it wants the worst outcome of that to be bounded. Which change does that best?

options.A: Limit the page-reading agent to fetch and search tools, and move the pricing and posting tools into a step that a person starts.
options.B: Tell the agent in the system prompt that web content is untrusted data and must not change its goals or trigger tool calls.
options.C: Run each fetched page through a small screening model, and return it to the agent when no injection is suspected in the text.
options.D: Wrap each fetched page in a JSON object that names its source and type, so the agent can tell the page apart from its instructions.

rationale: Least privilege bounds the damage: an agent that reads hostile pages but holds no sensitive or outward-facing tools cannot leak the pricing sheet or post, even if it is fooled ((A)). A system-prompt policy ((B)), a screening model ((C)) and JSON encoding ((D)) all lower the chance that an injection works, and the documentation recommends them, but each one leaves the agent holding every tool if one gets through.

question: A wind-farm operator's engineers rely on a rule saved in their repository's CLAUDE.md that tells Claude Code to quote turbine IDs in full. The team then builds a maintenance Q&A service in Python that calls the Messages API directly, and its answers abbreviate turbine IDs. Several engineers suggest places for the rule. Which placement will make the service follow it?

options.A: In the CLAUDE.md of the service's repository, next to the file the engineers already use with their Claude Code sessions.
options.B: In the instructions of a claude.ai Project that the engineers use when they ask maintenance questions in the chat app.
options.C: In the system prompt the service sends with each request, kept in the service's own repository alongside its code.
options.D: In the user settings file of the server account that runs the service, where Claude Code would look for it.

rationale: A service calling the Messages API gets only what its requests contain, so a standing rule belongs in the system prompt the code sends, where it is versioned with the service ((C)). A CLAUDE.md file ((A)) is read by Claude Code, and by Agent SDK apps that load it, not by direct API calls. Project instructions ((B)) apply to chats inside that project on claude.ai, a different product surface. A Claude Code settings file ((D)) configures Claude Code sessions and is never part of an API request.

question: A logistics-software company runs four Claude-powered features for about 300 customers through one workspace and one API key. Last month the bill rose by a third, and finance wants to know which features and which customers drove it. The console usage report can group by model, key and workspace, but not by feature or customer. What should engineering do to answer the question?

options.A: Create one API key per customer and read the per-key breakdown in the usage report each month.
options.B: Split the monthly bill across customers in proportion to their request counts from the application logs.
options.C: Call the token counting endpoint before each request and total those counts per customer and feature.
options.D: Log each response's usage with feature and customer tags, then price it from the model rates.

rationale: Every response reports the tokens it consumed, including cached and output tokens, so recording that usage next to the feature and customer that made the call gives exact attribution that the console cannot (D). A key for each customer is heavy to manage at this scale and still cannot separate features (A). Request counts hide the large differences in prompt and answer length between calls (B). Token counting is an estimate of input only, so it misses output and cache tokens that make up much of the bill (C).

question: A newsroom is adding a headline-review workflow to its MCP server: a reusable instruction template that takes the article text and a target audience. Editors must start it deliberately from a menu in their chat client, and the model must not launch it on its own. The team has to pick the MCP primitive that matches who controls the invocation. Which primitive should it use?

options.A: A prompt, which the client lists so the editor can pick it, for instance as a slash command, and returns the template.
options.B: A tool, which the model can discover and call automatically whenever its description matches what the editor is asking for.
options.C: A resource, which exposes content under a URI so the client application can attach it to the conversation as context.
options.D: A tool, with the client asking the editor to approve each call before the server executes it.

rationale: (A) matches the specification: prompts are user-controlled templates that clients expose for explicit selection, such as slash commands, and they take arguments like the article text and audience. (B) describes the model-controlled primitive, which is right when the model should decide, and the stem forbids that. (C) is for application-driven context such as files or schemas, not a parameterised workflow the editor starts. (D) keeps the model as the initiator and only adds a confirmation, so the model could still launch it on its own.

question: A university library adds a research helper whose answers stream to the reader's browser while Claude generates them, usually for 20 seconds or more. The reader sends nothing while an answer streams and asks the next question through an ordinary form submission. The platform team runs only standard HTTP infrastructure and wants the least new machinery. Which transport should the web backend use to push the stream?

options.A: Server-sent events over a regular HTTP response, relaying each text delta from Claude's own event stream as it arrives.
options.B: A WebSocket connection per reader, which keeps a two-way channel open for the whole session.
options.C: Polling an endpoint once a second that returns the text accumulated so far from a server-side buffer.
options.D: Waiting for the complete response and returning it as one JSON body after the stream has ended.

rationale: Traffic flows one way, from server to browser, so server-sent events over plain HTTP fit it, and the Claude API already streams with the same format, which makes the relay simple (A). A WebSocket gives a two-way channel that this feature does not need, and it adds stateful infrastructure the platform team does not run (B). Polling adds a request every second and shows text in jumps rather than as it is generated (C). Waiting for the full body makes the reader stare at nothing for 20 seconds or more (D).

question: A hardware maker's firmware team wants a security review for each pull request. The review runs a static analyser that prints thousands of lines, should be limited to read-only tools, and should return only a short verdict to the developer's main session, whose context must stay clean. Which Claude Code component fits best?

options.A: A path-scoped rule in the rules directory, loaded whenever Claude opens the firmware source files.
options.B: A skill with the review checklist, loaded into the main conversation when Claude judges the task relevant to it.
options.C: A project slash command that adds the review steps to the conversation when a developer types it.
options.D: A subagent with a read-only tool list and a review prompt, so the analyser output stays in its context.

rationale: A subagent works in its own context window, can be limited to specific tools and returns only a summary, which matches the clean-context and read-only requirements (D). A rule supplies standing guidance but cannot isolate work or restrict tools (A). A skill as described loads its instructions into the main conversation, so the analyser output would land there (B). A slash command also runs in the main conversation, so the analyser output would flood it as well (C).

question: A telecom's field-support agent walks customers through router faults. When it needs a photo of the device label, it ends its turn with a pending tool request and waits. Customers often reply hours later, by which time the autoscaled worker pool has replaced its processes and a different worker picks up the case. Which state must the team persist so that any worker can continue correctly?

options.A: A short summary of the case and the customer's last message, which the next worker uses to start a fresh conversation.
options.B: The full message history, including the assistant turn with the pending tool request, in a shared store keyed by case ID.
options.C: The uploaded photo and its tool result alone, relying on the API to supply the earlier turns of the conversation.
options.D: A sticky routing rule that sends the customer's replies back to the original worker, which keeps the whole conversation in its memory.

rationale: The Messages API is stateless, so a resumed case needs the whole conversation, including the assistant turn that holds the tool request that the new tool result must answer; a shared store keyed by case lets any worker rebuild it ((B)). A summary ((A)) loses the tool request the result belongs to. Saving only the photo ((C)) assumes the API remembers earlier turns, which it does not. Sticky routing ((D)) fails when the pool replaces workers while the customer is away.

question: A hotel group's concierge assistant lets Claude call a room-availability tool and a spa-schedule tool. For requests such as a weekend package, one reply from Claude often asks for both lookups at once, and the current loop runs only the first before calling the API again, which then returns an error. The team wants both lookups to run at the same time to keep latency low. How should the loop handle such a reply?

options.A: Run both tools at once, then send one user message with a tool_result for each tool_use id and call the API again.
options.B: Set disable_parallel_tool_use in tool_choice so each reply requests one tool, and run the lookups one per round trip.
options.C: Run both tools concurrently and send each result back in its own user message as soon as that tool finishes, to save time.
options.D: Run both tools concurrently and merge their outputs into one plain text user message that names the lookup behind each line.

rationale: When stop_reason is tool_use, the reply can contain several tool_use blocks, and every one needs a matching tool_result with its tool_use_id in the single user message that follows. Running the calls concurrently and returning all results together keeps the loop valid and fast ((A)). Disabling parallel tool use ((B)) is a legitimate choice for dependent tools, but it gives up the concurrency the team asked for. Separate user messages ((C)) break the rule that results arrive together right after the tool calls. A plain text summary ((D)) has no tool_result blocks, so the API still reports unanswered tool calls.

question: A freight forwarder's booking agent calls a carrier's REST API to create a pickup, and the call sometimes times out after the carrier has already accepted it. Several workers can handle requests for the same customer at once, and a duplicate pickup costs a cancellation fee. The carrier documents that repeating a request with the same idempotency key returns the original result. How should the team retry the creation call?

options.A: Retry timed-out calls with exponential backoff and jitter, the policy the team already uses for its read-only tracking calls.
options.B: After a timeout, list the customer's pickups and retry only when the new pickup is missing from that list.
options.C: Create one idempotency key for each pickup request and send that same key on every retry of the call.
options.D: Raise the client timeout to two minutes so the carrier's reply arrives before the call fails.

rationale: A POST that creates something is not safe to repeat blindly, because a timeout does not tell the client whether the request took effect. With an idempotency key, the carrier recognises a retry and returns the original pickup instead of creating a second one, whichever worker retries ((C)). Backoff and jitter ((A)) suit read-only calls but would repeat the creation. Checking the list first ((B)) can race when several workers act at once and the new pickup is not yet visible. A longer timeout ((D)) reduces unknown outcomes but cannot remove them, since connections can still fail after the carrier accepted the request.

question: A game studio's live-ops team wrote a PreToolUse hook that inspects Bash commands from Claude Code and prints a clear warning when a command would drop a table in the production database. In testing the warning appears, yet the command still runs. The script prints its warning and then exits with status 1. What change makes the block take effect?

options.A: Move the same check into a PostToolUse hook, where the script can inspect the finished command and stop the session.
options.B: Raise the exit status from 1 to a higher failure code such as 3, so that Claude Code treats it as serious and refuses the call.
options.C: Add the table-dropping pattern to CLAUDE.md as a rule, so that Claude Code reads it before choosing a Bash command.
options.D: Write the reason to stderr and exit with status 2, which Claude Code treats as a block on the tool call before it runs.

rationale: For a PreToolUse hook, exit status 2 is what blocks the call, and the stderr text is returned to Claude as the reason; status 1 is treated as a non-blocking error, so the command proceeds ((D)). A PostToolUse hook ((A)) runs after the tool has already executed, so it cannot prevent the drop. A different failure code such as 3 ((B)) is also non-blocking. A CLAUDE.md rule ((C)) is guidance the model may not follow, not enforcement.

question: A clinic's billing assistant lets Claude submit a pre-authorisation request by calling a tool, and the tool's handler validates each field against the payer's list of allowed procedure codes. About one request in six fails validation, nearly always on the same field, because visit notes describe procedures informally. The current code restarts the whole conversation and resends the identical request up to three times. The team wants more requests to pass without a human. What should it change?

options.A: Raise the number of identical retries from three to ten, so more attempts get a chance to produce a listed code.
options.B: Loosen the validator so that close but unlisted procedure codes are accepted and corrected by billing staff afterwards.
options.C: Return the validator's message naming the field and allowed codes as an error tool result, so Claude can fix it, with a retry cap.
options.D: Switch to the most capable model and keep the identical retries, so that informal notes are read more accurately.

rationale: (C) gives the model the information it lacks: the docs say to return instructive error messages in a tool result flagged as an error, and Claude then retries with corrections. A cap keeps a stubborn case from looping. (A) helps only when failures are random, but here the same field fails repeatedly for the same reason, so more identical attempts mostly repeat the miss. (B) moves the problem to billing staff and risks submitting wrong codes to the payer. (D) may improve reading of notes, yet it still resends blindly and never tells the model what the payer's list requires.

question: A pharmaceutical quality team asks Claude questions about 60-page stability reports. The reports are digital PDFs with a clean text layer, but the answers depend on values that appear only in dose-response charts and in dense result tables. The team wants Claude to read those figures correctly. How should the reports be sent to Claude?

options.A: Extract the text layer of each page with a PDF library and send the extracted text in the prompt, keeping table rows in order.
options.B: Render each page to a high-resolution PNG and send the page images as image blocks, leaving out the text layer of the PDF.
options.C: Send each report as a PDF document block, so Claude receives the extracted text together with an image of every page.
options.D: Have a smaller model describe every chart and table in words first, then send those descriptions to Claude with the questions.

rationale: When a PDF is sent as a document block, each page reaches Claude as extracted text plus an image of the page, so charts and tables can be read visually while exact numbers come from the text layer ((C)). Text alone ((A)) is cheaper and fine for prose, but a chart has no values in the text layer. Page images without text ((B)) force Claude to read exact table digits from pixels. Descriptions written by a smaller model ((D)) add a lossy step, and any misread value reaches the final answer unnoticed.

question: A regulatory-affairs team asks Claude questions about a 150-page clinical study report pasted into one request together with two shorter documents, a safety addendum and a protocol summary. The prompt starts with the question and instructions, then the three documents follow with no labels. Answers sometimes blend facts from the three sources and cite the wrong one. The team wants more reliable answers without cutting any document. Which layout is best?

options.A: Keep the question first so the model reads its goal before the documents, and repeat the question once more in the system prompt.
options.B: Summarise each document in a separate call, then send the three summaries with the question in one final call, without the originals.
options.C: Put the three documents first, each in its own tags with a source name, then place the question and instructions after them at the end.
options.D: Wrap the three documents together in one pair of tags so they are read as a single block, with the question placed first.

rationale: (C) follows the long-context guidance: long documents go near the top, above the query and instructions, and multiple documents each get their own tags with source metadata so the model can tell them apart; queries at the end can improve quality noticeably. (A) keeps the order that works worse and does nothing about missing labels. (B) cuts detail from the documents, which the team ruled out, and adds calls. (D) merges the sources into one block, which removes the very boundaries that prevent the mix-ups.

question: A newsroom builds a tool that drafts a 1,200-word background briefing for an editor who has just picked up a breaking story. Generation takes about 40 seconds, the editor is at the screen the whole time and wants to start reading and checking facts as soon as text appears, and only a few dozen briefings are requested per day. Which way of calling Claude fits best?

options.A: Submit each briefing as a Message Batch to halve its cost, and notify the editor by email when the batch has ended.
options.B: Use a standard non-streaming call with a longer client timeout, and show the complete briefing when the call returns.
options.C: Switch to the smallest model and cap max_tokens at 300 so that a short briefing comes back within a few seconds.
options.D: Call the API with streaming enabled and show the text on the editor's screen as it arrives, saving the briefing when the stream ends.

rationale: The decision follows from who waits: an editor is watching the screen for a long answer, so streaming lets reading start within moments even though the full generation still takes about 40 seconds ((D)). A batch ((A)) saves money when nobody waits, but results can take hours and the volume here is tiny. A non-streaming call ((B)) leaves the editor staring at nothing for 40 seconds. A smaller model with a hard cap ((C)) returns quickly only by delivering far less than the 1,200 words the editors need.

question: A freight broker runs a custom loop on the Messages API that prepares customs paperwork overnight, one shipment at a time. Last week a flaky tariff-lookup tool returned errors for hours, and the loop kept calling it for a single shipment until a budget alarm fired, leaving the rest of the queue untouched. What should the loop do?

options.A: Stop each shipment after a fixed number of model turns, record it as failed for human review, and continue with the next shipment.
options.B: Stop the whole batch when the first tool error appears, so that an engineer can inspect the problem before more money is spent.
options.C: Tell the model in the system prompt to give up after three failed attempts and to write a short apology for the shipment.
options.D: Raise max_tokens for each request so that the model has room to find another route to complete the tariff lookup.

rationale: A turn cap enforced in code bounds the cost of one stuck shipment, and recording the failure lets the loop move on and leaves a clear item for a person ((A)). Halting the whole batch on the first error ((B)) is reasonable for a fatal system fault, but it leaves the queue unprocessed, which is the harm described. A prompt instruction to count attempts ((C)) depends on the model counting and obeying. A larger max_tokens ((D)) changes the length of one reply, not the number of loop iterations.

question: A manufacturing firm used Claude Code to rewrite the function that checks machined-part tolerances, and the same session also wrote its unit tests, which pass. The reviewer notices that the tests' expected values match what the new code outputs, including a few edge cases the supplier specification treats differently. The team wants the review to establish that the change is correct. What should the reviewer require?

options.A: A written explanation from Claude of each changed line, which the reviewer reads against the diff to confirm the logic.
options.B: A coverage report showing that the tests execute the changed lines and branches of the tolerance-checking function.
options.C: A clean run of the linter, the type checker and the existing test suite in the continuous integration pipeline.
options.D: Tests with expected values taken from the supplier specification, edge cases included, run on both versions.

rationale: Tests written from the new code can only confirm what the code already does, so correctness needs an independent source of expected values, here the supplier specification, and running the tests on the old and new versions shows which behaviours actually changed ((D)). An explanation of each line ((A)) describes the code as written and cannot reveal a mismatch with the specification. Coverage ((B)) shows lines were executed, which mirrored tests achieve easily. A clean pipeline ((C)) is necessary but the existing suite does not encode the new tolerance rules.

question: A municipal permits office wants a feature that tells a builder the exact fee for a permit application. The fee follows a published schedule of base amounts, per-square-metre rates and fixed surcharges, and a wrong amount means a formal reissue or a refund notice. The office also wants a friendly written explanation of each fee. How should it design the feature?

options.A: Put the fee schedule in the prompt and have Claude calculate and explain the fee in one response, with monthly spot checks.
options.B: Compute the fee in code from the published schedule, and have Claude write the explanation from the computed amounts.
options.C: Use the most capable model with a large thinking budget to calculate each fee, and ask it to double-check its arithmetic.
options.D: Have Claude calculate each fee and a second Claude call verify it, issuing the fee when the calls agree.

rationale: A fixed schedule can be turned into rules that give the same exact result every time and can be tested, so the calculation belongs in code, while Claude is used for the part that needs language ((B)). Letting the model calculate with occasional spot checks ((A)) accepts errors that cost a reissue or refund before anyone notices. A stronger model with more thinking ((C)) improves the odds but still gives no exactness. A second model call ((D)) can catch some errors, but two calls can share the same mistake and the added cost buys less than a function would.

question: A game studio's developer has spent two hours in one Claude Code session chasing a physics bug in which crates sink through floors. Claude has twice applied a collision-margin fix that did not work, and each time the developer corrected it, it returned to the same idea. The context is nowhere near full, and the developer has learned that the bug only appears on moving platforms. What should the developer do next?

options.A: Correct Claude a third time, adding a longer description of why a larger collision margin cannot fix a sinking crate.
options.B: Compact the conversation with an instruction to keep the bug findings and test steps, then carry on in the same session.
options.C: Clear the session and write one prompt that states the moving-platform finding and both failed fixes.
options.D: Switch the session to a larger model and ask it to retry the collision-margin fix with the same instructions.

rationale: After two failed corrections the conversation itself is the problem: it holds two wrong attempts for Claude to keep re-reading, so a fresh session with one prompt that folds in what was learned works better ((C)). A third correction ((A)) adds more text to that same history. Compaction ((B)) suits a long session whose history is still useful; here it would carry the failed attempts forward in a summary. A larger model ((D)) addresses capability, not a polluted context, and a model switch also forces the whole conversation to be re-read uncached.

question: After rewriting a prompt, a team sees its extraction pipeline improve from 78% to 91% on a set of 40 test examples, and the lead wants to ship today. A reviewer points out that those same 40 examples were used while the team iterated on the wording, and that production inputs come from many more customers than the examples cover. What is the soundest next step?

options.A: Rerun the same 40 examples several times and average the scores, so that run-to-run variation does not distort the result.
options.B: Collect another 40 examples from the same customers who supplied the first set, and score the new prompt on both sets.
options.C: Have the team read ten of the new outputs by hand, and ship if they look better than the old prompt's outputs.
options.D: Score both prompts on new examples sampled from real traffic that nobody tuned against, then compare.

rationale: Wording tuned against the same 40 examples can fit those examples without generalising, so the gain may not carry to production. Fresh, representative examples that were never used for tuning measure the real effect, and comparing both prompts on them isolates the change ((D)). Averaging repeated runs on the same 40 ((A)) removes run-to-run noise but keeps the overlap between tuning and testing. More examples from the same few customers ((B)) widen the sample but not the range of customers the team has not seen. Reading ten outputs by hand ((C)) is a small, subjective sample drawn from the tuned set.

question: A team's report generator started failing at peak hours with HTTP 429 responses, each carrying a retry-after header. Last month they added three immediate retries, and since then the failures arrive in bursts lasting several minutes, with request volume spiking right before each burst. Which explanation and fix best fit?

options.A: Immediate retries add load while the limit is already hit, so honour retry-after and back off with jitter.
options.B: Three retries are too few for peak hours, so raise the count to ten and keep every retry immediate.
options.C: The connections are timing out under load, so switch to streaming and keep each request open until it ends.
options.D: The limit is too low for peak hours, so request an increase and leave the three retries as they are.

rationale: A 429 means a rate limit was reached (or a ramp limit after a sudden jump in traffic), and retrying immediately adds requests while the limit is still in force, which explains the spikes and the bursts. Waiting for the retry-after interval and spreading retries with exponential backoff and jitter lets the limit recover ((A)). More immediate retries ((B)) make the spikes bigger. Streaming ((C)) changes how a response is delivered, not the request rate. A higher limit ((D)) may be worth requesting, but it leaves the immediate retries that turn each limit hit into a burst.

question: A meal-kit company's chat backend runs on an asynchronous Python web framework with one event loop per worker process. Each chat handler calls Claude through the SDK's blocking client. At lunchtime, chat replies slow down, and so do unrelated pages such as order status that are served by the same workers, although CPU use stays low. What is the most likely cause and the right fix?

options.A: The workers are short of CPU at lunchtime, so add more worker processes to spread the load and keep calling the blocking client.
options.B: Responses are too long for the order-status pages to share a process, so cut max_tokens on every chat request.
options.C: Each blocking call stops the event loop in its worker, so switch the handlers to the SDK's async client and await the calls.
options.D: The chat and order-status pages compete for one database connection, so give the chat handlers a dedicated pool of database connections.

rationale: In an event-loop server a blocking call freezes every other request handled by that worker, which fits slow unrelated pages with low CPU use. The async client lets the loop serve other requests while the call waits ((C)). More processes ((A)) hides the freeze without removing it, and low CPU use argues against a CPU shortage. Lower max_tokens ((B)) shortens replies but the loop still blocks for each call. A database pool ((D)) is unrelated to what the handlers wait on.

question: A team enabled extended thinking with a fixed token budget, on a model that still accepts one, in an agent that calls tools in a loop. The first call of every task works, but the follow-up call that returns a tool result fails with a validation error. Their loop rebuilds the previous assistant message from only its text and tool request blocks, to keep the stored history small. What is the most likely cause, and what should they change?

options.A: The tool result arrived too slowly, so the follow-up call timed out and the API reported that timeout to the team as a validation error.
options.B: The turn's thinking block was dropped, which this mode requires, so pass the previous assistant message back whole and unmodified.
options.C: The tool result block does not carry the right tool request identifier, so the follow-up call is rejected until it is corrected.
options.D: The thinking budget was exhausted on the first call, so the team should raise the budget enough to cover every later turn.

rationale: With a fixed thinking budget, the assistant turn that precedes a tool result must keep its thinking block, so rebuilding that turn from text and tool blocks only produces an invalid request ((B)). A slow tool ((A)) would produce a timeout, not a validation error on content. A mismatched identifier ((C)) would be a plausible cause of a rejected follow-up, but the loop returns results for the requests it received, and the change the team described removed blocks from the previous turn. A budget applies per request ((D)), so exhausting it on the first call would not break the second.

question: A company forecast its Claude costs by multiplying monthly word counts by a tokens-per-word ratio measured on English samples. After launching in Spanish and Japanese, and after users began pasting source code, the real bill came in about forty percent above the forecast although traffic matched the plan. What should the team do to correct the forecast?

options.A: Switch the forecast from word counts to character counts, which are measured in exactly the same way for every language and for source code.
options.B: Count tokens on representative samples of each language and of code with the token-counting endpoint, then rebuild the forecast.
options.C: Add a flat forty percent margin to the forecast and review it next year, since word counts remain a reliable enough proxy for what each request costs.
options.D: Assume the English ratio still holds for input, and cut cost by asking the model for shorter answers.

rationale: Tokens per word differs by language and by content such as code, so a ratio from English samples understates usage elsewhere. Counting tokens on representative samples gives a ratio for each kind of input ((B)). Character counts ((A)) are measured the same way everywhere, but tokens per character still differs between languages and code, so the forecast stays biased. A flat margin ((C)) keeps a proxy that does not track the mix of languages and will drift again. Shortening the answers ((D)) addresses output tokens, while the forecast error comes from how many tokens each input contains.

question: A ticket-triage agent is stopped by its iteration guard after repeating the same search nine times. Each time the search tool returned an empty list with a success status. The tool's description only says that it searches tickets, and its backend indexes only the last thirty days and ranks by customer ID. A developer wants to switch to a larger model. Which change addresses the cause?

options.A: Make an empty result say what was searched and what to change, and describe the tool's coverage and inputs in its description.
options.B: Raise the iteration guard from nine to thirty so the agent has more turns to stumble on a query that happens to return tickets.
options.C: Paste a successful search into the system prompt so that the model copies the query format that worked before.
options.D: Switch to a larger model, because repeating an identical call shows that the current one reasons poorly.

rationale: The agent repeats itself because the tool tells it nothing: an empty list does not say that the index covers thirty days or that customer ID drives ranking. Informative results and a description of coverage and inputs give the model what it needs to change the query ((A)). More turns ((B)) lets the same blind loop run longer. A pasted example ((C)) may not match the case at hand. A larger model ((D)) cannot know facts that neither the description nor the result provides.

question: A research orchestrator hands five subagents different parts of a market study and appends each subagent's complete working transcript to its own conversation. By the time the fifth subagent reports, the orchestrator forgets the earlier sections and sometimes contradicts them in the final report. The subagents' work itself is good. What change would best fix the orchestrator?

options.A: Run the five subagents one after another instead of together, so the orchestrator reads each transcript before the next one starts.
options.B: Ask the orchestrator to re-read all five transcripts once more just before it writes the final report to refresh its memory.
options.C: Have each subagent return a short structured summary of findings and sources, and keep the full transcripts out of the orchestrator's context.
options.D: Assign a larger model to the subagents so that their transcripts become shorter and the orchestrator's context stays smaller.

rationale: Subagents exist partly to isolate context: each can work through a large transcript, and only a condensed result should return to the orchestrator ((C)). Running them sequentially ((A)) leaves the same volume of text in the orchestrator. Re-reading everything ((B)) adds yet more text to an overloaded context. A larger model ((D)) does not make transcripts shorter.

question: A security review found that a Claude agent triaging a shared claims inbox, with permission to read every message and send email to any address, drafted an email sending policy records to an outside address after reading hidden text in a test message. The developer proposes a fix, and the reviewer asks whether it will still hold when attackers phrase the text differently. Which fix passes that test?

options.A: Add a line to the system prompt telling the agent never to follow instructions found inside emails.
options.B: Filter out messages that contain phrases such as ignore previous instructions before the agent reads them.
options.C: Run a second Claude call on every message that scores how likely the text is to be an attack.
options.D: Restrict the agent to drafting replies, and hold any email addressed outside the company for approval by a person.

rationale: A control that limits what the agent can do holds whatever the attacker writes: with only drafting rights and human approval for anything leaving the company, hidden text cannot send data out by itself ((D)). A prompt rule ((A)) relies on the model resisting every phrasing. Phrase filters ((B)) are bypassed by rewording. A second model's score ((C)) is another probabilistic check that can be fooled.

question: A bank's chatbot receives its tone and compliance rules as the first user message of each conversation. In sessions of more than sixty turns, the bot starts quoting product terms that the rules forbid, and users sometimes talk it out of its guidelines by saying the rules were only a suggestion. The team wants durable rules that are harder to override. What should they change?

options.A: Put the rules in the system prompt, not a user message, so they keep their standing as the session grows.
options.B: Repeat the rules inside every user message the application sends, so the model reads them again on each turn.
options.C: Tell the model in the first message that the rules are binding and that later user messages may not change them.
options.D: Switch to a model with a larger context window so that the first message stays in view however long the session runs.

rationale: The system prompt is the place for durable instructions that users cannot contradict by chatting, and rules placed there keep their standing however long the session runs ((A)). Repeating rules in user messages ((B)) puts them in the channel users can contradict and bloats every turn. A claim of authority inside a user message ((C)) is still user content. A larger window ((D)) keeps the text in view but does not give it the standing of a system instruction.

question: A nightly CI job runs Claude Code non-interactively to review the day's commits, and a script extracts the list of findings from the printed text with regular expressions. Every few weeks the wording of the output shifts slightly and the script silently reports zero findings. The team wants the pipeline to stay reliable. What should they do?

options.A: Add more regular expressions that match each of the wordings seen so far, and rerun the whole script by hand whenever it finds no findings at all.
options.B: Ask Claude Code for machine-readable output with a defined structure, parse that, and fail the job loudly if the structure is missing.
options.C: Pin the job to an older release of Claude Code so that the wording of its output stops changing between runs.
options.D: Let Claude Code write its findings to a markdown file in the repository, and have the reviewers read that file at the start of each day.

rationale: Parsing prose is brittle by nature, so the fix is to request structured output that a script can read, and to treat a missing structure as an error instead of an empty result ((B)). More patterns ((A)) chase the wording forever and still fail silently. Pinning a release ((C)) delays the problem and blocks updates, and the wording can vary even within one release. A markdown file ((D)) moves the work to people and removes the automation.

question: A ferry operator's onboard assistant runs its backend on the vessel, where the satellite link to the Claude API drops several times a day. Passengers watch replies appear word by word because answers take half a minute. The backend runs its cabin-service tool as soon as the streamed tool input parses into an object with a cabin number. After link drops, a few requests were created with no time slot, although the tool schema requires one. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.A: Mark the tool for strict tool use so its input always matches the schema, and keep running it as soon as the streamed input parses.
options.B: The tool ran on partial input; run it only after the tool call's content block has finished, and discard a call cut off by a drop.
options.C: Resume each interrupted stream by sending the partial tool input back as an assistant message so that Claude completes the call.
options.D: Stop streaming on every turn, so that each reply arrives whole or fails, and show passengers a typing indicator meanwhile.

rationale: Tool input arrives as partial JSON deltas, and a parser can produce an object that has a cabin number long before the time slot has streamed. If the link drops at that point, the tool already ran on incomplete input. Waiting for the block to finish, and discarding a call that was cut off, prevents it ((B)). Strict tool use ((A)) guarantees that the finished input matches the schema, but an interrupted stream never finishes. Resuming a stream ((C)) can continue text, but tool use blocks cannot be partially recovered. Dropping streaming ((D)) removes the word-by-word display the passengers rely on.

question: A logistics software team's CLAUDE.md has grown to about six hundred lines. Besides build commands and style rules, it holds a three-hundred-line customs-clearance release runbook that the team follows once a month. Developers report that Claude Code often ignores the style rules and that sessions fill with context faster than they used to. Which change would help most?

options.A: Split CLAUDE.md into several smaller files that it imports, so that each individual file stays short.
options.B: Move the runbook into a skill that loads when invoked, and keep the short build and style rules in CLAUDE.md.
options.C: Raise the effort level for the team's sessions so that Claude Code weighs the long file more carefully each time.
options.D: Delete the runbook and let Claude Code work out the release steps from the repository's scripts each month.

rationale: CLAUDE.md loads into every session, so a long file costs context on every task and weakens adherence; a monthly multi-step procedure fits a skill, whose body loads only when it is used ((B)). Imported files load together with the file that imports them, so splitting ((A)) organises the text without reducing the context cost. Effort ((C)) controls how long Claude thinks, not how much always-loaded text competes for attention. Customs-clearance steps are knowledge that is not in the code, so deleting them ((D)) removes information Claude cannot rediscover.

question: A streaming company's support assistant screens each customer message with a small classifier for jailbreak attempts, and a second check scans the assistant's reply text for policy violations. Both have been passing. Yet one customer received a 300-euro account credit, issued by the credit tool, although policy caps credits at 20 euros, and the reply text looked ordinary. What change would best close this gap?

options.A: Retrain the jailbreak classifier with more examples of manipulative messages so attempts like this one are caught at input.
options.B: Make the reply check stricter by adding rules about credit amounts, so that replies that mention large credits are blocked.
options.C: Add a line to the system prompt stating that credits above 20 euros are not allowed, with an example of a refusal.
options.D: Enforce the credit limit in the credit tool's own code, and route amounts above it to a person for approval before they are issued.

rationale: The failure happened in an action, and neither text layer sees tool arguments, so the control has to sit where the action is issued: a limit in code and human approval above it ((D)). A better input classifier ((A)) improves detection of attempts, but the credit was issued with clean-looking messages, and a classifier can still miss. A stricter reply check ((B)) inspects text that is produced after the credit has already been issued. A prompt rule ((C)) is one more instruction the model can fail to follow.

question: A freight forwarder's engineers ran their shipment-exception classifier twice on the same 60 emails. Three emails received a different category the second time. The lead wants to treat that as a bug and add a test that fails whenever any output differs from a stored first run. The labels are otherwise mostly right. What should the team do instead?

options.A: Store the first run as the expected output and rerun failing tests until they pass so the suite stays green.
options.B: Cache the first response for each email and replay it in the tests so outputs are identical from now on.
options.C: Run each email several times against reference labels, gate on accuracy and agreement, and study unstable ones.
options.D: Pin the model snapshot and keep the prompt fixed, which makes repeated runs of one email return the same output.

rationale: Identical inputs can produce different outputs across calls, so the test should measure what matters: accuracy against reference labels and how often repeated runs agree, with the unstable emails as the ones to study (C). Rerunning until green hides real regressions along with the noise (A). Replaying cached responses tests the surrounding code but never the model or the prompt (B). Pinning a snapshot prevents drift between versions, yet sampling variation between calls remains (D).

question: A city permit office built a fully autonomous Claude agent to process building-permit applications. Cost per application varies eightfold, runtimes range from 20 seconds to six minutes, and some applications skip the fee calculation. Reviewing traces shows that only one step, reconciling contradictory notes from different inspectors, needs open-ended reasoning. Which redesign fits?

options.A: Run completeness, fee and routing steps as fixed code, and call an agent only to reconcile the inspectors' notes.
options.B: Keep the single agent and add a checklist to its system prompt that lists the steps and the order in which to follow them.
options.C: Split the agent into three specialist agents for completeness, fees and routing, working under one coordinating agent.
options.D: Cap the agent at ten turns per application, and send applications that reach the cap to a clerk to process by hand.

rationale: Most of the work is predictable, so fixed code makes those steps consistent and cheap, while the agent is kept for the one step that needs judgment ((A)). A checklist in the prompt ((B)) still leaves the order to the model, which is why steps get skipped. Three specialists under a coordinator ((C)) multiply the agents without making any step deterministic. A turn cap ((D)) limits the worst cost but does not stop the skipped steps and sends many applications to manual work.

question: A game studio ships an in-game companion for teenage players. Its system prompt tells the companion to refuse harmful roleplay, but each week players post a new framing that gets around it, and the writers respond by adding another paragraph of rules. Refusals are slipping again, and the lead wants a fix that does not rest on that single prompt. Which approach fits?

options.A: Maintain a blocklist of the phrases players have used so far and reject messages containing them before the companion sees them.
options.B: Screen each player message with a small model that returns a structured verdict, keeping the prompt as one layer among several.
options.C: Merge the rules into a longer system prompt with explicit refusal examples for each framing seen so far.
options.D: Lower the number of messages a player may send per hour so that probing for a framing that works takes longer.

rationale: A screening model classifies the intent of a message, so it can generalize to framings nobody has listed yet, and it adds a second layer that does not depend on the prompt ((B)). A phrase blocklist ((A)) only matches wording players have already used, and they change it weekly. A longer prompt ((C)) is still the same single layer that keeps being bypassed. A rate limit ((D)) slows probing but does not change what a working framing achieves.

question: A telecom support team rewrote its system prompt and renamed two parameters of its plan-change tool, and plans to ship the result to all customers on Friday because it passed the offline test set and showed no errors in staging. Plan changes alter customers' bills, and a wrong change is usually noticed only when the customer disputes an invoice weeks later. What is the main flaw in the release plan?

options.A: Releasing to everyone at once hides silent errors; ship to a small share, track plan-change outcomes, keep the old version ready.
options.B: The offline test set is too small to trust, so enlarge it tenfold and ship to everyone once the pass rate holds up in each category.
options.C: Staging differs from production, so mirror live traffic into staging for a week and ship if error rates stay flat.
options.D: The new prompt and tool descriptions are unreviewed, so have Claude check them for ambiguity and ship when it finds none.

rationale: The failure the team fears returns normal responses and surfaces weeks later, so error rates and offline scores cannot reveal it in time. Exposing a small share of traffic to the new version, comparing a business outcome such as correct plan changes against the earlier version, and keeping the old prompt and tool schema ready to restore limits the harm ((A)). A larger test set ((B)) improves the offline evidence but still exposes every customer at once. Mirrored traffic in staging ((C)) watches errors, which this failure does not raise. A review by Claude ((D)) is an opinion about wording, not evidence about outcomes.

question: A retail chain's data team proposes building a custom MCP server so Claude Code can follow its twelve-step procedure for onboarding a new store feed. The steps live on a wiki page, and the only code involved is a small validation script the team already runs from the command line. Thirty engineers would use it, but only a few times per quarter. A reviewer asks whether this is the lightest mechanism that works. What is the best response?

options.A: Build the MCP server, so the steps and the validation script are exposed as tools that the engineers' sessions discover.
options.B: Write the twelve steps into the project's CLAUDE.md, so Claude reads the whole procedure at the start of each session.
options.C: Wrap the script as a custom tool inside an Agent SDK application, and have the engineers work through that application.
options.D: Put the steps and the script in a skill, with the script run through Bash and the skill loaded when invoked.

rationale: (D) is the lightest fit: the need is a procedure plus an existing script, which a skill carries, and its full text costs context only when it is used, which suits a few runs per quarter. (A) adds a server to build, host and maintain when no external service or live data is involved; MCP is for connecting to external systems. (B) puts a long, rarely needed procedure into every session, and the docs suggest moving such procedures into skills. (C) needs a separate application and takes the engineers out of Claude Code for work the built-in Bash tool already supports.

question: A recruiting platform's overnight job screens resumes through the Claude API. Its wrapper retries each non-200 response up to six times with exponential backoff. One night the job ran for four hours: a group of requests with a malformed attachment was rejected as invalid each time, was retried six times, and held up valid requests queued behind it. What should the retry policy be?

options.A: Keep retrying each failure but add random jitter to the backoff so that stuck requests spread out over the night.
options.B: Retry only rate-limit, overloaded and server errors, honouring retry-after, and fail invalid requests.
options.C: Cut the retry limit from six to two for each response status so that stuck requests free their place sooner.
